Stilly.biography: The defining chapter of Stilly’s Fellas story is the 2023 championship, followed by a return trip to the title game in 2024. Nicknamed the Portfolio Manager, Stilly has earned a reputation for reshaping a roster midseason rather than waiting for a draft to pay off. Moves involving Mike Evans, Derrick Henry and Chase Brown form part of that story; Jayden Daniels later became a keeper investment. The defining tension of this franchise is constant reinvention: the moves do not always look tidy in isolation, but the trophy case proves at least one version came together when it mattered.

JMid.biography: JMid arrived as the Blockbuster Rebuilder, a manager willing to make the kind of deal that redraws a roster overnight. The 2024 season showed the upside: an 8–6 record and a documented league-high 1,730.22 points for. Acquiring and moving players such as James Cook, Kyren Williams and Calvin Ridley helped define the approach, while Ja’Marr Chase and Joe Burrow show up prominently in the credited starter archive. The Fellas record book still awaits JMid’s first championship, but the franchise has already demonstrated that its ceiling can match the league’s best.

Tom.biography: Four documented championships make Tom the standard every other Fellas résumé must answer. The original three-peat from 2016 through 2018 turned one successful season into a dynasty; the 2024 title proved that era was not the end of the story. Tom’s roster-building has often looked less spectacular in isolated transaction grades than in the season-ending results. Tee Higgins and Christian McCaffrey headline his recorded player contributions, but the defining figure is the manager behind four trophies. When the Fellas debate greatness, Tom starts with the simplest statistic: championships.

Stew.biography: Nobody embodies the restless side of fantasy management quite like Stew, the Fellas’ Day Trader. The 2022 team went 11–3 and led in both points and potential points, showing how formidable a roster the constant dealing can produce. His archive includes major acquisitions involving Justin Jefferson, Ja’Marr Chase and Puka Nacua; it also includes trades that invite second-guessing. The fascinating part of Stew’s legacy is the gap between roster construction and the trophy case. He has assembled elite regular-season teams without yet turning that volume of moves into a documented championship.

Scott.biography: Scott’s Fellas résumé is short in seasons but enormous in consequence. The 2025 championship arrived with a commanding documented title-game margin, putting a trophy on the shelf while longer-tenured managers were still chasing their first. The Converter earned the nickname by turning usable lineups into results rather than relying on constant blockbuster activity. Bijan Robinson anchors the recorded starter-production story, supported by productive contributions from James Cook and others. The unanswered question is not whether Scott can win a title—the 2025 season settled that—but how large the legacy can grow with more seasons.

Mitch.biography: Mitch has made the regular season look almost like an engineering problem. The Math Problem builds lineups around elite anchors and repeatedly produces overwhelming weekly output. His 2025 team finished 13–1 and scored 1,894.88 points in the archived season summary, one of the clearest demonstrations of the method. The recorded starter archive features Deebo Samuel, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Josh Allen and Jonathan Taylor. Yet the résumé carries a conspicuous blank: no documented championship. That contrast between week-to-week dominance and postseason payoff is central to the Mitch story.

Tony.biography: Tony’s 2021 championship is the cornerstone of a franchise built around calculated moves rather than constant noise. Known as the Quiet Poker Player, he has found value through trades, waivers and draft choices, often converting smaller transactions into meaningful lineup production. The archive highlights a 2021 deal involving Joe Mixon, James Robinson and Zack Moss, and later waiver activity that kept the roster flexible. Lamar Jackson, Jonathan Taylor and Stefon Diggs appear among the players who delivered in his starting lineup. Tony’s story is less about winning every argument and more about assembling one winning season.

Stover.biography: Stover’s reputation as the Asset Vault reflects a preference for valuable roster pieces and deep talent, not just a single weekly explosion. The franchise’s history includes a 2022 championship and a strong 2024 regular season in the broader team archive. Past source seasons also involve changes in the ownership of the roster slot, so the player-level Mount Rushmore intentionally credits only starts attributable to the documented owner. That distinction matters: the championship résumé is a historical franchise story, while the currently verified individual player archive is narrower. Future reconciliation should bring those two views closer together.

Kuhl.biography: Kuhl’s résumé is one of the Fellas’ most intriguing contradictions. The Process / Results Paradox has repeatedly uncovered useful talent—Kyren Williams in 2023 and J.K. Dobbins in 2024 are notable names in the transaction story—yet the documented championship column remains empty. Patrick Mahomes, Alvin Kamara and other productive starters populate the historical lineup ledger. Kuhl’s franchise invites a debate familiar to every fantasy player: when a manager makes good moves but does not get the corresponding final results, what deserves the credit and what deserves the blame?

Birch.biography: Birch’s 2019 championship established that the Blackjack Player can turn a willingness to gamble into a winning result. The 2021 regular-season run of 11–2 added a different kind of evidence: this franchise can be consistent as well as daring. The historical archive contains notable positional trades and draft values, while Josh Allen and Justin Jefferson lead much of the credited lineup story. Birch has become a perfect figure for Fellas debates because the decisions can look bold—or reckless—until the outcome is known. The title remains the strongest answer to those arguments.
